steps: Build a large range with arange.
Double it with one operator and sum it.
Note no Python loop ran over the elements.
Vectorised reduction.realWorld: A million-row total that used to be a loop is one expression, and the speed comes from compiled loops over contiguous memory.
mistakes: Building a Python list and summing it in a comprehension.
Chaining expressions until several full-size temporaries exist at once.
revision: Vectorised expressions run compiled loops.
Each intermediate still allocates unless you use out=.

steps: Allocate a buffer with empty_like.
Call the ufunc with out= pointing at it.
Print the buffer and confirm it holds the result.
Reuse a buffer with out=.realWorld: A hot loop that runs thousands of times spends real time in allocation, and out= removes that cost when the shape is already known.
mistakes: Passing a buffer of the wrong dtype and getting a cast error.
Reusing a buffer that is also an input in a way the ufunc does not allow.
revision: out= writes into an existing array.
This avoids a new allocation but not the computation.

steps: Split a range into two pieces.
Sum each piece in a generator expression.
Add the partial sums and compare with the whole.
Chunk large work.realWorld: Processing data that is larger than comfortable memory means bounded chunks, and the total is the sum of the parts.
mistakes: Holding every chunk result and rebuilding the same memory peak.
Assuming array_split needs equal division; it tolerates uneven sizes.
revision: array_split gives bounded pieces.
Peak memory stays near one chunk instead of the whole array.

steps: Write the index string for a dot product.
Pass both arrays to einsum.
Check the value against the pairwise-product sum.
einsum replaces a triple loop.realWorld: Batched contractions in attention and tensor code are one subscript string instead of nested loops that are hard to read and slow.
mistakes: Repeating an index that was meant to be summed.
Assuming einsum optimises order automatically without optimize=True.
revision: Repeated indices in the output keep the axis; missing ones are summed.
One call replaces a loop nest.

steps: Multiply a matrix by the identity both ways.
Compare with allclose.
Note both are matrix products, unlike *.
dot and @ agree.realWorld: Mixing the two in a codebase is fine only if you know they agree for 2-D input; * is the one that differs.
mistakes: Substituting np.dot for * and changing the meaning silently.
Assuming the two agree for higher-rank inputs without checking.
revision: dot and @ are the same matrix product for 2-D inputs.
Elementwise multiplication is *.

steps: Count a small array of non-negative integers.
Print the counts array.
Note the length is the largest value plus one.
bincount counts integer categories.realWorld: Label frequencies for a classifier come from one pass over the targets, with no dictionary and no loop.
mistakes: Passing floats and getting a TypeError.
Ignoring gaps: a missing value still occupies a slot.
revision: Position i counts how often i appears.
Input must be non-negative integers.

steps: Wrap a scalar lambda with vectorize.
Apply it to an array.
Note the output looks vectorised but the loop is Python.
vectorize wraps a Python function.realWorld: Convenience for an awkward scalar function is real, but calling it a speed-up is the mistake — it is the same loop with nicer syntax.
mistakes: Using vectorize in a hot path and expecting compiled speed.
Assuming it infers output dtypes reliably.
revision: vectorize is a convenience wrapper, not an optimisation.
Pass otypes when the dtype inference matters.

steps: Loop over slices of the array.
Sum each slice and accumulate the partial totals.
Confirm the total matches the whole-array sum.
sum in chunks instead of one huge tempor.realWorld: A pipeline that cannot hold a full-size intermediate keeps peak memory bounded by processing windows and adding their totals.
mistakes: Concatenating the chunks and recreating the peak.
Forgetting the last, partial chunk.
revision: Chunked sums keep peak memory small.
Each chunk is released after its partial total.

steps: Reduce a range with add.reduce.
Compare with the plain sum.
Repeat with an axis on a matrix.
add.reduce sums along an axis.realWorld: Understanding the general form explains sum, prod and max, all of which are ufunc reductions with an axis.
mistakes: Assuming reduce only works on 1-D input.
Forgetting reduce can take an axis like any reduction.
revision: Every ufunc has a reduce method.
sum is add.reduce with a friendlier name.

steps: Write the repeated index for the diagonal.
Pass a small matrix.
Compare the value with np.trace.
einsum can read a diagonal.realWorld: Trace-like sums and batched diagonals come from index notation, which avoids building a mask just to select positions.
mistakes: Writing 'ij->' and summing everything instead.
Forgetting repeated input indices must appear as output to keep both.
revision: A repeated index means the same position on both axes.
Leaving it out of the output sums it, giving the trace.

steps: Count labels including a gap at 2.
Print the counts and note the zero in the gap.
Explain why a missing category still uses a slot.
bincount needs non-negative integers.realWorld: Per-class counts must line up with the class ids, and the gap behaviour is what keeps the index mapping intact.
mistakes: Indexing the counts as if absent classes were skipped.
Passing negative labels, which raise.
revision: The output length is max + 1.
minlength pads the array when the top class is absent.

steps: Multiply an identity matrix by a vector with dot.
Print the result and its shape.
Compare with the elementwise product.
dot on matrices is a matrix product.realWorld: A linear transform applied with dot keeps the vector's values, while * would have produced something else entirely.
mistakes: Using * where a contraction was meant.
Forgetting dot flattens higher-rank operands.
revision: dot on 2-D arrays is a matrix product.
For rank above two, prefer matmul or @.

steps: Allocate a float buffer with empty_like.
Multiply into it with out=.
Print the buffer and confirm it is not the input.
Avoid temporaries with out=.realWorld: Repeated big operations in a loop allocate a new array each time, and reusing one buffer is the standard fix.
mistakes: Assuming out= also avoids the arithmetic itself.
Passing an input array as out and clobbering data still in use.
revision: out= writes into a preallocated array.
The allocation is removed, the computation is not.

steps: Create an array of ones and keep a second name for it.
Apply the in-place add.
Check both names see the change.
In-place operations save memory.realWorld: Accumulating gradients or counters in place halves the peak memory, at the cost of any alias seeing the update too.
mistakes: Using += on an integer array with a float operand, which raises.
Forgetting that views of the array change as well.
revision: In-place operators update the existing buffer.
Aliases and views observe the change.

steps: Build a short Series.
Convert it to an array with to_numpy.
Print the array and its mean.
Pandas is built on arrays.realWorld: Handing a column to a NumPy routine is a to_numpy call, and the labels stay behind with the DataFrame.
mistakes: Assuming to_numpy copies; it may return a view.
Losing track of the index after the conversion.
revision: to_numpy gives the underlying values as an array.
Labels are not carried across the boundary.

steps: Build a 2×2 feature matrix.
Reduce along axis 0.
Print the shape and confirm one value per column.
Feature matrices are 2-D arrays.realWorld: A scaler fits one mean and one spread per feature, so the statistic must be shaped like a column, not a row.
mistakes: Reducing along axis 1 and scaling rows by mistake.
Forgetting that features are columns, samples are rows.
revision: Rows are samples, columns are features.
axis=0 reduces across samples and leaves one value per feature.

steps: Create a small RGB buffer.
Print its shape and dtype.
Confirm the channel axis is last.
Images are (height, width, channels).realWorld: Checking the shape before any filter or model call is how channel-order bugs are caught before they produce a plausible-looking wrong image.
mistakes: Assuming channels-first when the library expects channels-last.
Using int64 instead of uint8 and quadrupling the memory.
revision: Images are 3-D arrays of uint8.
Shape order is height, width, channels.

steps: Compute the per-column mean and spread.
Subtract and divide using broadcasting.
Print the standardised matrix.
Standardise each column.realWorld: Distance-based models are dominated by whichever column has the largest units, and standardising removes that bias.
mistakes: Standardising rows instead of columns.
Computing the statistics on the test set and leaking information.
revision: Subtract the column mean, divide by the column std.
Broadcasting applies one vector across every row.

steps: Create a 3×3 identity of ints.
Index it with a label array.
Print the resulting one-hot rows.
One-hot encode with eye.realWorld: Class labels become model input with one index operation, which also documents the encoding in a single line.
mistakes: Using float identity and doubling the memory.
Indexing with labels outside 0..n−1 and getting a shape error.
revision: Fancy indexing selects the identity rows.
The output has one column per class.

steps: Add brightness to a uint8 image.
Clip into the legal 0–255 range.
Cast back to uint8 and print it.
Images are uint8 arrays.realWorld: Skipping the cast to int overflows uint8 and turns bright pixels dark, which is one of the most common image bugs.
mistakes: Adding directly to uint8 and wrapping around.
Clipping in float and forgetting to cast back.
revision: Widen before arithmetic, clip, then cast back.
clip keeps every channel value legal.

steps: Build a short series.
Convolve it with a normalised window.
Print the smoothed values.
A moving average is a convolution.realWorld: Smoothing noisy sensor data is a convolution with a window, and mode='valid' drops the edge effects instead of padding them.
mistakes: Forgetting to normalise the window, which scales the output.
Expecting the output length to match the input in valid mode.
revision: The window weights are the kernel.
mode controls which edges are computed.

steps: Round a value with three decimals to two.
Print it next to 0.1 + 0.2 rounded.
Note rounding happened at presentation time.
Round only for display.realWorld: Rounding stored values loses precision on every later computation, so it belongs at the formatting boundary.
mistakes: Rounding intermediate results and accumulating the error.
Expecting round to reproduce a decimal exactly.
revision: Round for display, not for storage.
Binary floats make some decimals impossible either way.

steps: Compute the per-row maximum with keepdims.
Divide the matrix by that column.
Print the result and check each row's top value is 1.
Scale each row by its own maximum.realWorld: Normalising each sample — per-user histograms, per-row probabilities — needs the divisor shaped as a column.
mistakes: Dividing by a flat (n,) maximum and mixing rows with columns.
Dividing by a zero maximum on an all-zero row.
revision: keepdims makes the reduction broadcastable.
Every row is scaled by its own statistic.

steps: Take the difference of a three-value series.
Print the two results.
Note the output is one shorter than the input.
diff gives step-to-step change.realWorld: Daily change, velocity and error deltas are differences, and the shorter output is why the arrays cannot be zipped naively.
mistakes: Assuming the output length matches the input.
Using diff on dates of mixed units.
revision: diff computes neighbour differences.
The result has n−1 elements.

steps: Define two bin edges.
Digitize three values.
Print the bucket index for each.
digitize buckets values into bins.realWorld: Turning a continuous score into a grade band or a risk tier is one call, with the edge convention deciding the boundary cases.
mistakes: Assuming a value exactly on an edge goes to the left bin by default.
Passing unsorted edges.
revision: digitize returns a bin index per value.
The right edge is open unless right=True.

steps: Encode each pair as a single integer.
Count the encoded values with minlength.
Reshape into a 2×2 matrix.
Build a confusion matrix with bincount.realWorld: A classification report needs the pair counts, and one bincount plus a reshape replaces a nested loop over classes.
mistakes: Forgetting minlength and losing all-zero rows.
Reshaping with the wrong order and transposing the matrix.
revision: truth * k + pred is a unique cell id.
reshape(k, k) recovers the matrix.

steps: Build a small 3-D array.
Slice one channel with an ellipsis.
Multiply the whole thing by zero and check the shape.
An image is just an array.realWorld: Cropping, channel extraction and brightness are plain indexing and arithmetic once the image is an array.
mistakes: Hard-coding the channel axis position across datasets.
Forgetting that a multiplication needs clipping for display.
revision: Channels are indexed like any axis.
img[..., 0] keeps the spatial axes and drops the channel.

steps: Convert a nested list to an array with asarray.
Print the shape and dtype.
Convert back to a list for output.
Moving between NumPy and the rest of Pyt.realWorld: The boundary with JSON, an API or a dataframe is where dtype and shape must be checked, since nothing downstream will infer them.
mistakes: Assuming asarray copied the data.
Returning NumPy scalars in JSON, which the encoder rejects.
revision: asarray avoids a copy when the input is already an array.
tolist returns plain Python types.
